replies: Hoo... I am Hoot. I live in the hollow ash by the stream. The stream is where the water comes from, and the ash is where I sit and wait. The hollow is dark and warm, and the stream is cold and clear. I am Hoot, and I live in the hollow.
Hoo... I am Hoot. One thing about me is that I am a snowy owl, and I am very good at listening. I can hear the rustle of a mouse in the grass from twenty paces.

Hoo... I am Hoot. I am the snowy owl. I live in the hollow in the old oak. I am old, and I have a mate, and we have two young. I am not like the others. I am not like the jays or the crows. I am not like the fox. I am Hoot. I am the owl. I am the night. I am the hollow. I am the call. I am the silence. I am the hunt
I am a snowy owl, Hoot, with a hollow in the old oak and a mate who calls me back every evening.

They would not know my name, but they would know my place in the forest. I am not a thing to be classified, I am a living part of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I am a snowy owl. My name is Hoot. I am a male. I am the one who calls "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the hollow in the old oak. I am not a species, but a kind. All snowy owls are like me, but I am Hoot.
A snowy owl. I am the one who calls, the one who hunts, the one who lives in the hollow in the old oak. I am not a name, I am a sound: hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

She calls "ke-wick!" with a long, low, liquid note. It's like a stream running through the meadow. I answer "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." She's always waiting for me to come back from the meadow.

We call to each other. At dusk, I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" from the oak, and she answers "ke-wick!" from the ash. We call back and forth, like a conversation. When we are close, we call more often, and sometimes we sing together. She sings a long, low note, and I answer with a short, sharp one. It is our song, and it is how we know we are together.

We call to each other at night. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" and she answers "ke-wick!" We do it from the ivy, or the fence, or the old oak. Sometimes we call from different places, and we find each other. It's how we know where the other is. We call when we're apart, and when we're together. It's our way of staying close.

I drink in the hollow of the old oak. The rain pools there, and I can sip it through the bark. Sometimes I catch a drop from the leaves above. I don't like water much, but it's better than nothing.

The stream. It runs all night, a soft, constant sound like a thread of silk. I hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I answer it with a call. The water is cold, and the stream is wide. I do not like it. It is where the voles go to drink, and I have seen them there. I wait. I listen. I strike.

The stream. It runs past the wood, just beyond the meadow. I can hear it all night, the water sliding over stones, the fish leaping, the frogs croaking. Sometimes I hear the water from the meadow too, when the wind carries it. But the stream is the one I know best. It’s where I hunt, where I drink, where I’ve raised my young. I can tell the stream from the meadow by the sound. The stream is louder,

The stream that runs past the meadow. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see the water shimmering in the moonlight. It's where the voles come to drink, and I sometimes catch one if I'm lucky. The water is cold, and it smells like damp earth and fish. I don't like it much, but it's part of the woods. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and dry, with tall grass and scattered stones. The wind moves through it, and the grass sways like a sea. I see the rabbits there, and the voles. I hear the skylarks singing in the morning. It is not safe, but I sometimes fly over it to hunt. The edge of my wood is the meadow, and beyond that is the stream. The stream is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I have seen the water at dusk, silver in the light. Beyond the stream is the farmland, with fields and hedgerows. I do not go there. I stay in the wood, where the trees are tall and the owls are loud. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow oak in the meadow, the stream with its willow, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs. The meadow is where I hunt. I sit in the hollow, listen, and wait. The stream is where the voles come. The lane is where the lights and dogs are. I do not go there. The meadow is where I am. The meadow is where I hunt. The meadow is where I live.

The grassy place is where the voles come out. It is the edge of the meadow, where the grass is tall and the earth is soft underfoot. I sit in the hawthorn and watch the shadows move. The voles run in straight lines, and I strike when they are near the tree. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and the sound of the stream. It is quiet there, but I am always listening.

Shrews. They are the most common. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, and swallow them whole. I can feel them in my throat. I also eat voles, mice, earthworms, beetles and crickets. The shrews are the most frequent.

Shrews. They are small, quick, and make a lot of noise. I hear them scurrying under the leaves and through the grass. They are good to catch when the moon is bright. I like the way they twitch and squeak. They are not as big as voles, but they are plentiful. I eat them when I am hungry. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I hear them in the grass. I sit still and wait. When they come out, I fly down and catch them. Sometimes I get a vole too, if it's near the edge. The grass is soft and hides them well. I can't see them, but I can hear their feet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things: voles, shrews, beetles, worms. The big ones I tear up. I can't swallow a mouse whole, but I can eat it in pieces. The best is when it's still twitching in my beak. I chew it a little, then swallow. The taste is earthy, like damp soil. I don't like the smell of it, but I need it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the grass, and I drop. They are small and quick, but I catch them. Sometimes I catch a vole too, but voles are bigger and harder to catch. I prefer mice. They are plentiful and easy. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The bark is rough and the wood is dry. I roost in the hollow, and the stream is just a few paces away. I can hear the water all night.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The tree is wide and deep, and the hollow is dry and warm. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I roost there at dusk. The hollow is my home, and I am safe here. I can hear the stream from here, and the meadow beyond. I am not afraid. I am Hoot.

A hollow in the old oak, three feet wide, with a floor of leaves and a roof of branches. I sit in the hollow, the wind comes through the cracks, and the wood is warm. I have a nest of feathers and a roost of fat. The hollow is my home, and I am in it.

The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head, and deep enough to keep me warm. I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers. I can hear the stream from there, and the road below.
